assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Section '1. Fulfillment Method Splitting' with dedicated table showing 'One pickup, one delivery: Camera (pickup), Tripod (delivery) | 2 shipments | {Camera}, {Tripod}'

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Section '2. Delivery Address Splitting' with dedicated table showing address-based splitting, e.g. 'Gift to a different address: Shirt (123 Main St), Toy (456 Oak Ave) | 2 shipments'

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Section '3. Availability-Based Splitting' with dedicated table showing 'One backordered: Shirt (in stock), Jeans (backordered May 1) | 2 shipments | {Shirt} immediately, {Jeans} May 1'

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: Section '4. Warehouse Allocation — Minimising Shipments' with dedicated table showing warehouse selection optimization, e.g. 'Two warehouses preferred over three' with 2 shipments chosen

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: Section '5. Companion Product Co-location' with dedicated table showing scenarios like 'Single warehouse stocks both companions: Camera body, Lens | Body ↔ Lens | 1 shipment | Chicago: body + lens | yes'

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 includes: 'All home delivery: Shirt (delivery), Jeans (delivery)', 'All store pickup: Camera (pickup), Bag (pickup)', and 'One pickup, one delivery: Camera (pickup), Tripod (delivery)'

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 includes: 'All to same address: Shirt (123 Main St), Book (123 Main St) | 1 shipment' and 'Gift to a different address: Shirt (123 Main St), Toy (456 Oak Ave) | 2 shipments'

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 includes: 'All in stock', 'One backordered: Shirt (in stock), Jeans (backordered May 1)', 'Both backordered, different dates: Shirt (backordered May 1), Jeans (backordered Jun 1)', and 'In stock + pre-order' scenario. Intro states 'backordered and pre-order items ship when available' treating them equivalently

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Table 4 includes: 'Single warehouse has full qty: Chicago: 6 | 1 shipment', 'Two warehouses needed, clean split', 'Two warehouses preferred over three' (2 shipments over 3), and 'Total stock insufficient: Cannot fulfill'

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Table 5 includes: 'Single warehouse stocks both companions' (first scenario) and 'No warehouse stocks both companions' (fourth scenario with unavoidable split: Chicago: body, LA: lens). However, no scenario shows fulfillment impossible due to one companion being completely unavailable at any warehouse—all companion scenarios involve both items being available somewhere.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenario names are descriptive: 'All home delivery', 'One pickup, one delivery', 'Gift to a different address', 'Both backordered, different dates', 'Two warehouses preferred over three', 'Co-location is a tie-breaker between equal-shipment options'. None use generic labels like 'Test case 2'

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Tables use explicit item-property notation: 'Shirt (delivery), Jeans (delivery)' in Table 1; 'Shirt (123 Main St), Toy (456 Oak Ave)' in Table 2; 'Shirt (in stock), Jeans (backordered May 1)' in Table 3. Each item name has its properties in parentheses, making mapping unambiguous

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 uses 'Qty ordered' column with scalar values (6, 4, 6, 6, 6, 6) and 'Warehouse stocks' shows quantities: 'Chicago: 6', 'Chicago: 6, LA: 3, Houston: 1' rather than item names

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column names across all tables use business language: 'Cart items', 'Shipments?', 'Groups?', 'Warehouse stocks', 'Allocation?', 'Companion pair', 'Companions together?' — all domain-appropriate and readable by product stakeholders

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns consistently use question marks: 'Shipments?' and 'Groups?' in Tables 1–3; 'Shipments?', 'Allocation?', and 'Companions together?' in Tables 4–5, while input columns ('Scenario', 'Cart items', 'Warehouse stocks') lack question marks

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Table 4: 'Two warehouses needed, uneven split' — 6 items needed, Chicago stock: 4, LA stock: 4, allocation 'Chicago: 4, LA: 2' uses available inventory; 'Cannot fulfill' — 6 needed but only 5 total available (2+2+1). Table 5: 'No warehouse stocks both companions' — body assigned to Chicago (which has it), lens to LA (which has it)

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Three 'Open questions:' sections surfaced: Table 3 with 2 questions (backorder date handling, early shipment opt-out); Table 4 with 2 questions (tie-breaking criteria, per-item vs order-wide application); Table 5 with 3 questions (companion availability conflicts, multi-item companion sets, fulfillment method boundaries)
